title: Practical skills or academic subjects at school
prompt:
Some people think that schools should teach children practical skills, such as cooking and managing money. Others believe that academic subjects should remain the priority.

Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
tips: Give your opinion clearly in the introduction and keep it consistent through to the conclusion.
Spend one body paragraph on each view, developing one or two ideas fully rather than listing many.
A third body paragraph can show your own position, for example a compromise, if you explain it.
Support ideas with specific examples, such as students who move away from home.

samples.text:
Nowadays many people discuss about what schools should teach. Some people think that practical skills like cooking and managing money are important, but other people believe that academic subjects should be the priority. In this essay I will discuss both views and give my opinion.

On the one hand, practical skills are very useful in the life. For example, many young people leave home to go to university and they don't know how to cook, so they eat fast food every day and this is bad for their health. Also, managing money is important because a lot of young people have debt with credit cards. If schools teach these skills, students will be more independent and they can avoid many problems in the future.

On the other hand, academic subjects like maths, science and languages are necessary for get a good job. Universities and companies look at students' grades in these subjects, so if schools spend time for cooking, students will have less time to study. In addition, parents can teach their children to cook at home, but most parents cannot teach physics or chemistry.

In my opinion, I think academic subjects should be the priority but schools should also teach some practical skills. For example, they can have one lesson every week about money. This way, students can get good grades and also learn useful skills for life.

In conclusion, both practical skills and academic subjects are important. Although academic subjects are more important, schools should teach both of them so students are ready for the future.
samples.commentary:
Band 6 overall.
Task Response (6): Both views are discussed and an opinion is given, but the position is slightly unclear: the body says academic subjects should be the priority, while the conclusion says 'schools should teach both'. Ideas are relevant but some are underdeveloped (the debt example is asserted, not explained).
Coherence and Cohesion (6): Clear four-part structure and paragraphing. Linking is accurate but mechanical and formulaic ('On the one hand', 'Also', 'In addition'), and 'In my opinion, I think' is redundant.
Lexical Resource (6): Adequate vocabulary for the topic ('independent', 'priority') with some errors of word choice and collocation ('discuss about', 'in the life', 'have debt with credit cards', 'spend time for').
Grammatical Range and Accuracy (6): A mix of simple and complex sentences with conditionals, but errors such as 'necessary for get' and article/preposition slips are frequent, although they rarely reduce communication.

samples.text:
The question of what schools should teach has become increasingly contested. While some argue that children ought to learn practical skills such as cooking and handling money, others maintain that traditional academic subjects must come first. In my view, academic subjects should remain the core of the curriculum, but a limited amount of practical teaching is both valuable and necessary.

Those who favour practical skills point out that many young adults leave school unable to look after themselves. Students who move away to university often survive on takeaway food because they have never learned to cook, and a lack of financial knowledge can lead them into debt that takes years to repay. Supporters of this view argue that schools are the only place where every child, regardless of family background, can be guaranteed to learn these basic life skills.

On the other hand, there are strong reasons for keeping the focus on academic study. Subjects such as mathematics, science and languages provide the foundation for further education and most skilled careers, and they are far harder to learn informally than cooking. Moreover, school timetables are already crowded, so every hour spent on practical lessons is an hour taken away from subjects in which students will be formally assessed.

Personally, I believe the two aims are less opposed than they seem. Money management, for instance, can be taught within mathematics lessons through realistic problems involving budgets and interest rates, and basic nutrition fits naturally into biology. In this way, schools can give students essential practical knowledge without reducing academic standards.

In conclusion, although practical skills clearly matter, academic subjects should remain the priority, with practical content integrated into them wherever possible.
samples.commentary:
Band 7 overall.
Task Response (7): Both views are discussed in a balanced way, and a clear position is presented in the introduction and maintained throughout. The integration idea in the fourth paragraph is a thoughtful, relevant extension. Some support could be more specific; the point about debt is plausible but general.
Coherence and Cohesion (7): Logical progression with clear central ideas in each paragraph. A range of cohesive devices ('On the other hand', 'Moreover', 'for instance', 'In this way') is used appropriately, with occasional slightly formulaic choices.
Lexical Resource (7): Sufficient range to discuss the topic with some flexibility and precision ('contested', 'core of the curriculum', 'formally assessed', 'regardless of family background'). Collocation is mostly natural.
Grammatical Range and Accuracy (7): A variety of complex structures (relative clauses, 'every hour spent on... is an hour taken away from...') used with good control. Errors are rare. Band 8 would need more precise development of examples and wider lexical flexibility.

samples.text:
Few people would dispute that schools exist to prepare children for adult life; the disagreement lies in what that preparation should consist of. Some believe that practical competences such as cooking and personal finance deserve a central place in the curriculum, while others insist that academic disciplines must take precedence. I would argue that academic subjects should remain the priority, but that the most important practical skills can and should be taught within them.

The case for practical education is a compelling one. A school leaver who can solve quadratic equations but cannot plan a weekly food budget, or does not understand that a credit card charges interest on unpaid balances, is poorly equipped for independent life. Crucially, these skills are not distributed equally: children from well-off or well-organised households tend to absorb them at home, whereas others may never encounter them at all. Leaving such learning to families therefore risks widening existing inequalities.

Nevertheless, the argument for academic priority is, in my view, stronger. Mathematics, the sciences and languages are cumulative disciplines; a gap in understanding at the age of twelve can close off options at eighteen, and few of these subjects can be picked up later through casual experience. Cooking, by contrast, can be learned at almost any stage of life from books, videos or friends. Given that teaching time is finite, it would be a poor bargain to sacrifice hard-to-acquire knowledge for skills that are comparatively easy to acquire independently.

The apparent conflict, however, largely disappears if practical content is embedded rather than added. Compound interest is a far more engaging context for exponential growth than abstract examples, and the chemistry of baking or the biology of nutrition can make science lessons more concrete. Such an approach strengthens academic learning while ensuring that every student, not just the fortunate, leaves school able to manage the basics.

In short, schools need not choose between rigour and relevance: by keeping academic subjects at the centre and weaving practical skills into them, they can deliver both.
samples.commentary:
Band 8 overall.
Task Response (8): Fully addresses both views with well-developed, well-supported arguments, including a perceptive point about inequality. The position is clear from the introduction and consistently argued. The comparison of 'hard-to-acquire' and 'easy to acquire' knowledge is a strong, extended line of reasoning. Some readers might want a brief concrete example of the integrated approach working in practice, which keeps it from Band 9.
Coherence and Cohesion (8): Ideas are sequenced skilfully, and cohesion is managed naturally ('Crucially', 'Nevertheless', 'by contrast', 'The apparent conflict, however'). Paragraphing is purposeful.
Lexical Resource (8): Wide and precise vocabulary used fluently ('cumulative disciplines', 'take precedence', 'embedded rather than added', 'rigour and relevance'), with natural collocation and only very occasional slightly elaborate phrasing.
Grammatical Range and Accuracy (8): A wide range of structures, including complex noun phrases, conditionals and contrastive clauses, almost entirely free of error.
